newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian central bank acts to revive economy, exports.
newsitem.headline: Indian central bank acts to revive economy, exports.

text.p: India's central bank announced measures at the weekend to boost market liquidity and prompt interest rate cuts to help reverse a downtrend in industrial production, exports and stock markets.

In its monetary policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March), the RBI announced steps to boost liquidity, raise export credit and increase the flow of bank funds into stock and commodity markets.

It announced a cut of two percentage points in banks' cash reserve requirement (CRR) staggered over the next four months, releasing more than 85 billion rupees ($2.4 billion) into the banking system. Analysts said it was the strongest signal ever for a cut in interest rates and revival of industrial credit.
Bank of Baroda, a leading Indian bank, announced a 50 basis points cut in its prime lending rate to 15 percent after the RBI announcement. Other banks are expected to follow.
The RBI also cut the ceiling on interest for banks' deposits for maturities of 30 days to one year to 10 percent from 11 percent.

"A two percentage point cut in CRR will definitely ease the minds of bankers who have been fearing that liquidity will tighten in the near future," said K.R. Ramamoorthy, chairman and managing director of state-run Corporation Bank.
"This may have prevented interest rates from coming down in the past but they should definitely go down now," Ramamoorthy said. Banks could now lend more aggressively, he said.
"I think banks will now start marketing credit - which they never did before," said Anil Singhvi, treasurer of the private Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd.
"The increase in the availability of funds is timely," said S.H. Khan, chairman and managing director of long-term lender Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI).
"Not only has the availability of funds improved but the cost is also likely to come down," Khan said. "I see industrial production picking up in the second half of the year."
He expected industrial growth figures for the year to touch 10 percent. Growth in the first quarter of 1996/97 was 8.5 percent, the RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said.
Rangarajan also said the RBI's decision to allow Indian banks to lend expatriate Indians' dollar accounts to local firms would make $2 billion of fresh funds available to industry.
This is expected to have a steadying influence on the rupee against the dollar.

To boost exports, the RBI raised banks' export credit target to 12 percent of each bank's net credit from 10 percent. It also imposed a ceiling of 15 percent on interest on post-shipment credit beyond 90 days.
The RBI scrapped archaic credit controls on key commodities, including sugar, cotton and oilseeds.
"The move is unprecedented and a radical departure from the past," commodities analyst C.S. Aiyar told Reuters.
Depressed stock markets are expected to be boosted by the RBI's decision to allow banks to invest in corporate equity and debt in the secondary markets for the first time.
